narrative:
The model predicted a 69% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

Three factors drove this outcome, ranked by importance. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest influence; being in the bottom decile (compared to an average of roughly the sixth decile among accepted students) strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. Your LSAT score of 20 was the second most important factor. This is far below the average of 37 among students who were admitted, and it also pulled the prediction heavily toward failing the bar.

Your family income bracket came third. Being from a lower-middle income family actually worked slightly in your favor, since most accepted students come from upper-middle or middle brackets. However, this modest positive effect was not nearly enough to offset the much larger negative signals from your academic performance and test score.

Taken together, the model concluded that the combination of low class standing and a low LSAT created too high a risk of bar exam failure. To improve your chances on a future application, you should focus on raising your academic performance and, if possible, retaking the LSAT to reach a score closer to the typical range of admitted students. These two areas offer the clearest path to shifting a future prediction in your favor. (248 words)
